source_title: Carvana Co. - Form 10-K (Fiscal Year 2022) and 2023 Debt Exchange Disclosures
publisher_issuer: Carvana Co. (filed with U.S. SEC, EDGAR CIK 0001690820; corroborated by July/September 2023 8-K and company press releases)
company_context: Carvana is an online used-car retailer that grew revenue rapidly but carried heavy debt (partly from its 2022 ADESA acquisition) and burned cash. In 2022 a high-revenue base coexisted with a near-bankruptcy liquidity and debt crisis; a 2023 noteholder debt exchange materially cut debt and interest, enabling survival.
macro_context: 2022 rapid interest-rate hikes raised debt-service and floorplan financing costs, cooled used-car demand off pandemic highs, and shut high-yield markets, turning Carvana's leveraged growth model into an acute solvency scare.
outcome_category: 7 - high revenue but cash flow crisis
evidence_summary: Carvana generated full-year 2022 total revenue of about $13.604 billion (up ~6% year over year) yet posted a net loss of roughly $2.9 billion (commonly reported around $1.6B net loss attributable plus minority/structure effects; widely cited ~$2.9B total loss for 2022), with bankruptcy speculation through late 2022 driven by its debt load. In July 2023 Carvana announced an agreement with noteholders to reduce total debt outstanding by over $1.2 billion, eliminate more than 83% of its 2025 and 2027 unsecured note maturities, and lower required cash interest expense by over $430 million per year for two years; the exchange completed by September 2023 with 96%+ noteholder participation, cutting obligations by roughly $1.3 billion. 2023 net loss narrowed sharply (to roughly $450 million).

source_backed_metrics.net_loss_2022_usd: approximately 2.9 billion (also reported ~1.6 billion net loss attributable to Carvana Co.)
source_backed_metrics.annual_cash_interest_reduction_usd: over 430 million per year for two years

owner_decision_context: With a large revenue base but unsustainable debt service and a closed high-yield market, management chose to restructure debt out of court via a noteholder exchange (trading lower principal and deferred maturities for higher-coupon secured notes) rather than risk a Chapter 11 filing, while simultaneously cutting costs to reach positive adjusted EBITDA.
action_taken: Executed a July-September 2023 noteholder debt exchange reducing total debt by ~$1.2-1.3 billion, eliminating 83%+ of 2025/2027 unsecured maturities, and cutting cash interest by >$430M/year for two years, alongside operating cost reductions.
outcome_evidence: Despite ~$13.6B revenue and a ~$2.9B 2022 loss with bankruptcy speculation, the 2023 debt exchange (96%+ participation, ~$1.3B obligations cut) plus cost cuts narrowed the 2023 net loss to ~$450M and kept Carvana out of bankruptcy, confirming a high-revenue-but-cash/debt-crisis that resolved into survival.
source_limitations: WebFetch of sec.gov returned 403; figures confirmed verbatim in WebSearch snippets attributed to Carvana's FY2022 10-K, its July 19, 2023 noteholder-agreement press release, and corroborating named journalism (CNBC, CNN, Bloomberg, UPI, Motley Fool): revenue $13.604B (+6%), Q4 2022 net loss $806M, >$1.2B debt reduction (~$1.3B completed), >$430M/yr interest cut, 83%+ maturities eliminated, 96%+ participation, 2023 loss ~$450M. The 2022 full-year net loss is reported variously (~$1.6B attributable vs ~$2.9B total) so both framings are noted.
directly_stated: Full-year 2022 total revenue was approximately $13.604 billion, up about 6% year over year
Carvana posted a Q4 2022 net loss of approximately $806 million
In July 2023 Carvana agreed to reduce total debt outstanding by over $1.2 billion
The agreement eliminated more than 83% of 2025 and 2027 unsecured note maturities and lowered required cash interest expense by over $430 million per year for two years
The completed exchange had over 96% noteholder participation and cut obligations by approximately $1.3 billion
2023 net loss narrowed to approximately $450 million
inferred: Carvana's crisis was a debt/solvency and cash problem layered on a still-large and growing revenue base, not a demand or revenue collapse
The out-of-court restructuring plus cost discipline converted a near-bankruptcy condition into survival and partial recovery
why_useful_for_opsiq: Prime high-revenue-but-cash-crisis (outcome 7 into 3) case where a ~$13.6B-revenue, growing retailer is nearly sunk by leverage and interest burden, then survives via a governed debt restructuring. Tests whether the engine separates strong/growing revenue from debt-solvency distress and credits an out-of-court noteholder exchange as the correct phase action rather than misreading the situation as healthy growth.
